checks.claim: Key: a watershed is all the land that drains to one outlet, so land whose creeks run to a river that empties into the bay is in the bay's watershed, however near another body of water it lies
checks.note: USGS: 'an area of land that drains all the streams and rainfall to a common outlet'.

checks.claim: Premise: New York hills draining south to the Susquehanna (which empties into the bay) can lie far nearer to Lake Ontario than to the bay
checks.note: The Susquehanna rises at Otsego Lake near Cooperstown, NY, and enters the bay at Havre de Grace, MD; the basin covers parts of New York and holds over 30,000 farms, dairy among them. By latitude and longitude Cooperstown is roughly 95-100 miles from Lake Ontario's shore and about 230 miles from Havre de Grace, so the premise holds.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: 'The lake's, as the lake lies much nearer' (nearness does not set the watershed)
Wrong choice: 'Both, as it lies between the two' (a patch of land drains to one outlet; the Ontario and Chesapeake basins do not overlap)
Wrong choice: 'Neither, as it is far from both'
Context: rain and what it washes off the fields travel down the creeks and river to the outlet
Context: the bay's watershed is about 166,000 square kilometres in six states and the District of Columbia
checks.note: Grokipedia: 64,000 square miles (166,000 km2), parts of six states (DE, MD, NY, PA, VA, WV) plus DC.

checks.claim: Key: a watershed's edge (its divide) runs mostly along ridges and hilltops
checks.note: USGS: 'Ridges and hills that separate two watersheds are called the drainage divide.' Grokipedia (Drainage divide) adds that divides can cross low ground in flat country; the stem's 'hilly country' and 'most of the walk' cover that.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: banks of the river's creeks (the creeks run through the basin, not round its edge)
Wrong choice: edges of marshes and ponds
Wrong choice: floors of the valleys
checks.note: Valley floors are where the streams collect; in hilly country the divide keeps to the crests.

checks.claim: Context: rain on one side of a divide drains to this river, on the other side to the next
Context: North America's Continental Divide follows the Rocky Mountains, sending water toward the Pacific on one side and toward the Atlantic on the other
checks.note: Grokipedia: it follows 'the crest of the Rocky Mountains' and separates Pacific-bound water from water bound for the Atlantic (Gulf of Mexico included) and the Arctic. The sentence is true for the US stretch and does not say 'only'; an optional polish is 'toward the Atlantic and the Arctic'.

checks.claim: Stem: clay can have more than half its volume as pore space, more than gravel, sand or silt
checks.note: Wikipedia: porosity 'more than 0.5 for peat and clay' (about 0.51-0.58 for clay soils); sandy soil about 0.36-0.43; unsorted gravel about 0.20; solid granite under 0.005. Grokipedia (Porosity): clays 'up to 60%'. The stem also stipulates that the clay holds the most of these four layers.

checks.claim: Key: the gravel gives a well the most water (large, joined pores, high permeability)
checks.note: Bear (1972) chart: well-sorted gravel and sand 'pervious', silt 'semi-pervious', clays 'impervious'. A USGS specific-yield table gives clay an average specific yield of about 2% against about 21% for fine sand: clay holds water but gives little to a well.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the clay (high porosity, very low permeability)
checks.note: USGS: 'Groundwater moves very slowly through low permeability materials such as clay and shale.' Wikipedia (Porosity): 'clays typically have very low hydraulic conductivity'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the silt (grains between clay and sand; lets water through slowly)
checks.note: Silt is semi-pervious, orders of magnitude below gravel.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the granite (almost no pores; water only in cracks)
checks.note: Grokipedia: low-porosity rocks such as granites depend on fracture networks for any useful flow; Wikipedia: solid granite porosity under 0.005.

checks.claim: Context: clay's spaces are 'so tiny and poorly linked' that water barely moves
checks.note: Grokipedia (Aquifer): clay 'can exhibit low permeability if pores are fine and poorly connected'. A hydrologist would stress the tiny pore throats and water held on grain surfaces more than poor linking, but the plain-words version is the standard textbook one and not wrong.

checks.claim: Context: gravel is permeable as well as porous; a well in it refills fast
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'coarse gravels with lower porosity but large, linked intergranular spaces yield high permeability'. CK-12: a rock layer must be porous and permeable to be a good aquifer.

checks.claim: Key: the big well's pumping lowered the water table (cone of depression) below the shallow well
checks.note: USGS: 'Pumping a well lowers the water level in and around the well to form a cone of depression in the water table'; 'If the cone of depression extends to other nearby wells, the water level in those wells will be lowered'; when the level falls below the pump intake, wells 'will begin to pump air - they will go dry'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: drilling cut off an underground stream
checks.note: USGS: 'Some people think groundwater is like a large lake or river underground, but that isn't the case'; it is 'more like the liquid trapped in a sponge'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: pumping emptied the whole aquifer
checks.note: The cone is local and deepest at the pumping well; the ground below the lowered water table stays saturated.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: drilling shook loose mud into the well (would not make a well run dry while the water table holds)
Context: the cone is funnel-shaped and deepest at the pump; the ground deeper down stays soaked
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'localized cones of depression that can merge into regional drawdown'.

checks.claim: Context: groundwater fills spaces in soil and rock rather than flowing in underground streams
checks.note: Matches USGS's own wording; open channels exist only in caves, which this ground is not.

checks.claim: Context: the usual fix is to drill the shallow well deeper
checks.note: Penn State: a cone can 'lower the water table below the level of the well'; 'The only solution for this is to drill the well deeper'.

checks.claim: Key: paving means less rain soaks down to refill the groundwater
checks.note: USGS: impervious surfaces reduce 'the area where infiltration to groundwater can occur'. Texas 7.11A: impervious cover is inversely proportional to the rain that becomes groundwater.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: more rain soaks down
checks.note: Grokipedia: impervious surfaces impede natural recharge of groundwater. (Leaky pipes and lawn watering can add water underground in some cities, but that is not rain soaking in, so the choice stays wrong.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the paving's weight squeezes the water out
Wrong choice: nothing, as the water lies so deep
Stem: paving makes the creek flood higher after storms
checks.note: USGS: urbanisation brings 'more frequent and more severe flooding'.

checks.claim: Context: 70 to 90 percent of rain can run off in the most built-up places, against 10 to 20 percent in wild country
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'up to 70-90% of precipitation in highly urbanized areas compared to 10-20% in undeveloped watersheds'. TxDOT's rational-method table gives downtown business areas a runoff coefficient of 0.70-0.95 (https://www.txdot.gov/manuals/des/hyd/chapter-4--hydrology/section-12--rational-method/runoff-coefficients.html). The often-shown EPA/FISRWG water-budget figure gives 55% runoff for a watershed 75-100% paved and 10% for natural cover; the card's 'most built-up places' and 'can' keep it true.

checks.claim: Context: groundwater feeds creeks between storms, so paved towns often see creeks that run lower in dry spells
checks.note: Grokipedia reports baseflow falls of 20-50% in urbanised catchments, but Bhaskar et al. 2016 (USGS) find urban baseflow falls in some cities (Baltimore) and rises in others (Perth, from leaky pipes and infiltration). 'Often' is defensible; 'can' would be safer. Optional polish: 'so paved towns can see creeks that flood higher after rain and run lower in dry spells'.

checks.claim: Key: the dam's lake traps most of the river's sand and mud on its bed
checks.note: Grokipedia: reservoirs 'trap up to 90-100% of incoming bedload', trap efficiency 'often exceeding 80% in well-designed reservoirs'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: swept it out past the beaches into deep water
Wrong choice: ground it to dust in its turbines
Wrong choice: spread it over the fields along the river (the dam ends the floods that did this)
checks.note: Grokipedia: downstream farms lost 'the 1-2 cm annual silt deposition'.

checks.claim: Context: Lake Nasser holds back over 95 percent of the Nile's sediment
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'trapped over 95% of the river's sediment load in Lake Nasser'; the Aswan Dam page gives about 98%. 'Over 95' fits both.

checks.claim: Context: the dam was finished in 1970 and the Nile delta's shore has retreated faster since
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'completed in 1970' (dedicated January 1971); Rosetta promontory retreat rose from about 58 to about 125 metres a year after construction (Environmental impact of reservoirs).

checks.claim: Stem: a dead zone is water near the sea floor so low in oxygen that most fish leave or die; fertiliser from the watershed feeds it
checks.note: NOAA: 'Most marine life either dies, or, if they are mobile such as fish, leave the area'; nutrient pollution is 'the primary cause of those zones created by humans'.

checks.claim: Key: a wet spring most likely makes a larger dead zone, as more fertiliser reaches the sea
checks.note: 2019: heavy spring rain across the Mississippi watershed brought high discharge and nutrient loading; NOAA forecast 7,829 sq mi and measured about 6,952 sq mi, the eighth largest in 33 years, even after Hurricane Barry mixed the water. 'Most likely' is the right hedge.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: smaller, as the extra water thins the fertiliser
checks.note: The 2012 drought gave 'near record low levels of water traveling down the Mississippi', fewer nutrients and the fourth-smallest zone since 1985: low flow, not high flow, shrinks it.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: smaller, as the rainwater brings more oxygen
checks.note: More fresh water strengthens the layering that keeps oxygen from the bottom.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: about the same, as the rain falls so far from the sea
Context: algae grow, die and sink; bacteria rotting them use up the deep water's oxygen; fresh river water floats on the salty sea, so little oxygen mixes down
checks.note: NOAA NCCOS: 'the bacteria feeding on the dead plankton consume oxygen'; fresh water is less dense and sits on top, and 'this low-oxygen water is trapped under the fresh layer'.

checks.claim: Context: wet springs, as in 2019, bring large dead zones; the 2012 drought brought one of the smallest on record
checks.note: 2012 measured 2,889 sq mi, fourth smallest since mapping began in 1985 (NOAA); 2019 the eighth largest of 33 years. The record stays 8,776 sq mi (2017).

checks.claim: Stem: San Joaquin Valley farmers pumped groundwater for decades; by the 1970s the ground had sunk more than 8 metres in places
checks.note: USGS: farmers relied on groundwater 'beginning around the 1920s'; by 1970 'some areas had subsided by as much as 28 feet' (8.5 m). Grokipedia (Subsidence): 'exceeding 9 meters (30 feet) in some locations' from the 1920s to the 1970s.

checks.claim: Key: the clay packed tighter as the water was pumped out
checks.note: Grokipedia: pumping compresses 'fine-grained layers that contribute most to subsidence'; 'Coarse-grained sands and gravels compact less'. USGS: 'aquifer-system compaction and land subsidence'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: caves left by drained underground lakes fell in
checks.note: Sinkholes over caves are a karst (limestone dissolution) process, not one in valley sand and clay.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: weight of crops and farm machines
Wrong choice: earthquakes along a fault
checks.note: USGS attributes it to overpumping.

checks.claim: Context: pore water helps carry the ground's weight; drawing it out lets the weight press the clay grains together; the sinking is mostly permanent and the squeezed clay holds less water
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'permanent subsidence as particles rearrange and interlock', 'permanent loss of aquifer storage capacity'; USGS: 'permanent aquifer-system storage loss'.

checks.claim: Context: collapsing caves make sinkholes in limestone country; sand and clay hold no caves; groundwater does not lie in underground lakes
checks.note: USGS: groundwater is not 'like a large lake or river underground'. Cave lakes do exist in limestone, which the same sentence has just named, so an optional polish is 'and groundwater there does not lie in underground lakes'.

checks.claim: Stem: sardines are usually ready to breed by the end of their first year
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Sexual maturity is attained rapidly, usually by the end of the first year of life' (the European pilchard at about 1-2 years).

checks.claim: Stem: the orange roughy is a deep-sea fish that does not breed until at least 20 and may live more than a century
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'do not begin to breed until they are at least 20 years old'; ages of 149 years by radiometric dating, claims over 200. Grokipedia: maturity at 20-41 years, validated ages 93-149, depths about 500-1,500 m.

checks.claim: Key: the orange roughy population shrinks faster, as it breeds so late
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'slow-growing fish that reproduce late in life, such as orange roughy, are vulnerable to overfishing'; overfishing is removal faster than the species can make up by natural population growth.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the sardines', as more of them are caught (the stem fixes the same share)
Wrong choice: the sardines', as each lives only a few years (short life with early breeding means fast replacement)
checks.note: Grokipedia: a 'fast life-history strategy' emphasising early reproduction. Sardine stocks do boom and bust, but the comparison at an equal fishing share still favours the sardine.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: both alike, as each loses the same share
Context: sardines breed within about a year and spawn many times a season
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'spawning occurs in multiple batches over an extended season'.

checks.claim: Context: many orange roughy stocks were badly depleted within 3 to 20 years of fishing
checks.note: Wikipedia: many stocks 'became severely depleted within 3-20 years'.

checks.claim: Context: about a third of tracked sea fish stocks are overfished
checks.note: FAO figures: 34% (2017), 35.4% (2019), 35.5% or 37.7% (2021) depending on the base. 'About a third' holds; 'over a third' would be closer to the latest figures. The share rises slowly, so the wording should survive future reports.

checks.claim: Key: currents that slowly circle the ocean (the North Pacific gyre) gather the rubbish
checks.note: NOAA: 'The gyres pull debris into one location, often the gyre's center, forming patches'; the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is in the North Pacific Gyre.

checks.claim: Stem: the patch lies far from land, roughly midway between Hawaii and California
checks.note: NOAA: 'in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and California'; Wikipedia gives about 135-155 W, 35-42 N.

checks.claim: Stem: bottles, bags and lost fishing nets drift out to sea 'from coasts all around the Pacific'
checks.note: Bottles and bags do wash out from coasts, but the patch's nets (nearly half its mass, Lebreton 2018) and most of its identifiable hard plastic (75-86% from fishing, Lebreton 2022) come from fishing at sea, not from the shore. Suggested fix: 'Bottles and bags drift out to sea from coasts all around the Pacific, and fishing boats lose nets far out on it.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: tides that pull it away from the coasts
checks.note: Tidal currents are 'oscillating currents' that flow back and forth; they cannot herd rubbish to one spot mid-ocean.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: ships that dump their rubbish in that spot
checks.note: Ships add some debris, but the gathering is done by the gyre.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: waves that roll it out from the beaches
checks.note: Breaking waves drive floating things shoreward.

checks.claim: Context: winds and Earth's spin keep the surface water of each great ocean turning in a vast loop (gyre); floating rubbish drifts toward the calm middle and stays
checks.note: Grokipedia: gyres are 'driven primarily by prevailing winds and deflected by the Coriolis effect'; Ekman convergence 'directs buoyant materials toward the gyre interiors' and the circulation inhibits escape. There are five main gyres (North and South Atlantic, North and South Pacific, Indian), so the Pacific and Atlantic each have two loops; optional polish: 'keep the surface water of the great oceans turning in vast loops'.

checks.claim: Context: the patch is no floating island; most pieces by count are plastic smaller than 5 mm; a boat can sail through and see little
checks.note: NOAA: 'Patch is a misleading nickname'; 'mostly made up (by count) of plastic pieces smaller than 5mm'; 'possible to sail through some areas ... and see very little to no debris'.

checks.claim: Context: 'Tides only carry water in and out along the coasts'
checks.note: Tides are not only coastal: they rise and fall across the whole ocean (the open-ocean lunar tide is about half a metre), and tidal streams run offshore too, only weaker. What makes the choice wrong is that tidal currents swing back and forth and carry floating things nowhere for good. It also clashes with the T2 tides unit's bulges. Fix: 'Tides only slosh water back and forth, so they cannot herd rubbish to one spot far out at sea, and waves push floating things toward the shore, not away from it.'

checks.claim: Context: waves push floating things toward the shore, not away from it
checks.note: True of the waves breaking on a beach, as the choice describes.

unit_notes: All ten keys hold. One context error (Q 8ede77985c: tides described as coastal only) and one uncertain stem phrase in the same question (nets said to drift from coasts). Optional polish only: Q 041f490b4f Continental Divide also sends water to the Arctic; Q 2893f95960 'often' to 'can' for low dry-weather flow (urban baseflow rises in some cities); Q b168619348 'groundwater there' (cave lakes exist in limestone); Q 8ede77985c five gyres, not one per ocean. The eight checks the lead named (porosity vs permeability, the cone of depression, subsidence by clay compaction, paving and soaking in, dams trapping sediment and starving coasts, dead-zone size following spring flow, gyres and floating plastic, late breeders overfished more easily) all came out ok.
